problem: Visual navigation policies do not transfer across robots with different body sizes, camera intrinsics/extrinsics and camera types. Prior work needs massive multi-robot datasets or fine-tuning, and ignores robot geometry, so collision safety is not guaranteed. Monocular depth also suffers from scale ambiguity.
motivation: Laser-scan based policies (DRL-DCLP) transfer well across robot dimensions because scans are metric and normalized, while raw images are coupled to camera setup. Converting monocular RGB into a calibrated metric virtual laser scan should give the same embodiment invariance with cheap cameras and no retraining.
key_idea: Convert RGB to metric depth with an offline ArUco-based affine scale calibration of a relative-depth model, project it into a height-adaptive virtual 2D laser scan, and feed it to a dimension-configurable DRL planner (DRL-DCLP) for zero-shot cross-embodiment navigation.
insight: Reducing heterogeneous visual inputs to a geometric scan makes the policy embodiment-agnostic, so the planner is trained only in simulation on LiDAR. The depth table shows that the per-camera calibration reduces MAE substantially against uncalibrated metric-depth models (Depth Anything V2 Small indoor/outdoor 4.19/3.02 m vs 0.69 m for Ours+DAS). In simulation, the gap to LiDAR-based DRL-DCLP (SR 78 vs 83 at 0.5 m/s) is attributed to depth noise and limited FOV.
method: Offline scale calibration: detect ArUco markers of known size at near and far distances, solve PnP for corner metric depth, and fit the disparity affine map d_gt = s1*d_pred + s2 by ridge regression (closed form).
Online scale correction: apply D_metric = 1/(s1*F(I)+s2) to Depth Anything V2 relative-depth output (Small/Base/Large), with no retraining.

Visual-to-scan abstraction: back-project metric depth with intrinsics, transform to the robot frame with extrinsics (height/pitch), and keep points with h_min<z<h_max, where h_max is the robot's height, to filter ground and overhead points.
Virtual scan projection: convert points to polar coordinates, take the minimum range per angular bin, and use max range for empty bins to produce a unified laser scan.

Dimension-configurable planner: DRL-DCLP with PointNet encoding of per-point features (sin, cos, 1/(d-beta), L_front, L_rear, W/2) plus goal, velocity and dynamics limits, and a SAC policy trained by curriculum in ROS Stage.

Optional VLN high-level module: CLIP scores left/center/right image regions against the instruction and outputs (d_cmd, theta_cmd) by thresholds (0.65/0.80). CeRLP acts as the low-level obstacle avoider.

numbers_note: Real-world navigation and VLN results are only qualitative (trajectory figures); no SR tables. Simulation uses BARN, not a canonical benchmark.
results: In BARN simulation CeRLP gets SR 78.0% at 0.5 m/s and 70.0% at 1.0 m/s, beating DWA, Fast-DWA, E-Band (65.0%) and E2E, with the lowest timeout rate. It stays below the LiDAR-based DRL-DCLP (83.0%/73.0%). Scale correction cuts depth MAE to 0.59–0.69 m versus 1.15–4.19 m for VGGT-1B and metric DA-V2 baselines, and real robots (7 embodiments incl. quadruped) navigate collision-free qualitatively.
limitations: Real-world evidence is qualitative, with no quantitative success rates or baselines; the VLN module is very simple (CLIP, three regions).
Needs per-camera offline ArUco calibration and known extrinsics, and has a higher collision rate than LiDAR because of depth noise and limited FOV.
Robot modeled as a cuboid with 2D planar scan; the depth model is heavy on Large variants (162 ms).
